How to Prepare for the JLPT: 10 Evidence-Informed Strategies

Kanjidon Team · Jan 30, 2026

A JLPT result depends on language knowledge, reading, listening and execution under the official format. No trick can ensure a passing result, but preparation becomes more efficient when each activity answers a specific problem. These ten strategies focus on evidence, diagnosis and repeatable work rather than rigid timelines.

1. Choose the Level with Official Material

Read the official ability summary and try sample questions for the level. A third-party kanji total or course label is not enough. If the sample is mostly guessing, test the next lower level before building a plan.

2. Learn Kanji Through Vocabulary

Study a reading in a real word instead of memorising every possible sound for a character. Connect the written form, pronunciation, meaning and one sentence. That is closer to how language knowledge appears on the test.

3. Combine Retrieval with Spaced Review

Try to produce the answer before revealing it and revisit successful items after delays. Spacing and retrieval have research support, but no scheduler knows the exact moment you will forget and no interval locks a kanji in forever.

4. Contrast Grammar in Sentences

Group patterns that look similar and ask why one fits a sentence and another does not. Build your own minimal examples. Grammar lists become useful only when you can interpret their role in context.

5. Train Reading in Layers

Begin with short passages and identify topic, purpose and referents before translating details. Add time pressure gradually. For longer texts, practise locating claims and relationships instead of reading every line at one speed.

6. Listen Without Replay Sometimes

Use some practice where the audio continues and you must retain the task, speaker and key detail. Afterwards, inspect the transcript and replay the missed part. Repeated listening is useful for learning; first-listen practice is useful for diagnosis.

7. Learn the Current Test Structure

Use the official times and question composition for your level. N5 totals 90 minutes, N4 115, N3 140, N2 155 and N1 165 across their timed sections. Do not rely on an old book whose timing predates the N4, N5 or N1 changes.

8. Use Mock Exams as Diagnostics

A mock should reveal pacing and error patterns. Recreate the official section times, avoid dictionaries and record guesses. Then spend more time correcting the causes than taking another simulation immediately. Raw accuracy is not an official scaled JLPT score.

9. Protect Every Scoring Section

Passing requires the overall threshold and a minimum in each scoring section. Do not let a strong kanji deck hide neglected listening, or strong listening hide unreadable passages. Track each section separately.

10. Remove Test-Day Uncertainty

Read the local guide, confirm the venue and identification, prepare permitted stationery and sleep on a normal schedule. A light review may be useful; an absolute claim that nobody can learn in the final 24 hours is not. The priority is arriving able to execute what you already know.

How Kanjidon Can Help

Kanjidon can support kanji and vocabulary by JLPT level, spaced review and mock-style practice from its local question bank. Use the app for those tasks, then add grammar, broad reading and listening. Treat practice scores as feedback, not as a guaranteed or officially scaled result.

Official and Research Sources

  • Official JLPT test sections, question composition and times
  • Official JLPT results and pass marks
  • Official JLPT sample questions and practice workbooks
  • Karpicke and Roediger (2008): retrieval practice
  • Cepeda et al. (2008): spacing and retention intervals
